1: Our school has changed the starting time of the afternoon English class this month. The timetable on the office door confirms that lessons now begin at two instead of one. The staff have been preparing a second classroom for a larger group of students. I have noticed several extra chairs and some new books near the entrance. The group might be growing, although I have not asked the teacher about enrollment yet. I will check the updated timetable before arranging my journey next week. This change gives me enough time to have lunch before class without rushing across town.
2: I would like to take on the role of assistant at your community library. I can organize information clearly, and I can explain simple instructions to visitors patiently. In my previous volunteer role, I created a list that helped people find books more quickly. I am good at listening when someone is unsure how to describe the information they need. I would be happy to team up with experienced staff while learning the library's computer system. My next learning goal is to improve my spoken English when answering unexpected questions. I am ready to ask for feedback and practice new tasks until I can complete them confidently.
3: Our bus trip began an hour late, but Daniel and I remember the delay differently. I had arrived at the station before eight and had waited near the ticket desk. According to Daniel, the departure board still showed the original time when he entered the building. He had called the organizer earlier, so he expected someone to explain any changes. By the time the driver arrived, several passengers were asking whether the trip would be canceled. I thought the driver explained the problem clearly, while Daniel felt that the announcement was too brief. However, we both agree that nobody missed the bus because of the delay. Next time, we will check the organizer's messages before leaving home.
4: In my opinion, figure skating should be considered both a sport and an art. Skaters need strength and precise technique to perform difficult jumps safely during a competition. They also use music, movement and expression to communicate a mood to the audience. I think the physical demands are a strong reason to recognize skating as a sport. The creative choices in a performance give us an equally good reason to discuss its artistic qualities. Some people argue that scoring makes it a sport rather than an art, and I see your point about that distinction. However, a competition can still include creative expression as well as measurable skills. Could you explain why you think the two categories must be completely separate?
5: I am comparing a bus, a train and a rental car for a weekend trip to the coast. The bus is cheaper than the train, but the seats offer less room for a long journey. The train is more comfortable than the bus and passes beautiful scenery along the river. It is also the fastest option because it avoids the traffic near the city center. The rental car offers freedom to explore, but it is the most expensive choice after fuel and parking. Driving on unfamiliar roads would make the trip more stressful than exciting for me. For me, the train is the best option because I can relax and enjoy the view. I would spend the money I save on a guided walk at our destination.
6: To reach the science museum, start at the main entrance of the central station. Walk along River Street until you reach the small bridge beside the cafe. Cross the bridge and continue through the park, keeping the playground on your left. The museum is in a red building at the end of the path. According to the printed tourist guide, visitors should enter through the door facing the river. The website says that this entrance is temporarily closed and directs visitors to the side door instead. I trust the museum's website more because its notice includes today's date and details of the repair work. I would still check the signs when arriving in case the entrance changes again.
7: I recommend starting a short city tour at the market on River Street. It is worth visiting because you can see local foods and meet people who prepare them. After exploring the stalls, walk along the river toward the bridge near the old mill. Cross the bridge and look for the small museum in the square on the other side. You should visit it because its photographs explain how the neighborhood has changed over time. Finally, follow the path under the railway bridge to the public garden. You could finish the tour there because the shaded benches provide a comfortable place to rest. These three stops are close enough to visit without spending the whole morning on transport.
8: In my region, a simple bean stew is a familiar meal at family gatherings. It is made with beans, onions, garlic and vegetables chosen by the person preparing it. The beans are soaked beforehand so that the preparation is easier to organize the next day. The stew is cooked slowly until the beans are soft and the flavors have developed. It is served with rice, and different side dishes can be added according to each family's preferences. Fresh ingredients are used whenever they are available at the neighborhood market. People value this dish because a large pot can be shared easily around a crowded table. For my family, preparing it together is as important as eating the finished meal.
9: You should think carefully about your daily routine before adopting a pet from the local shelter. You may have enjoyed looking after your cousin's dog last summer, but a permanent responsibility is different. Your cousin must have trusted you because she left detailed instructions and asked you to help again. You have enough time for regular walks now, don't you? You will also need to plan for food, veterinary care and someone reliable to help during travel. Before adopting, ask the shelter about the animal's needs and whether they match your home. I would not choose a pet only because it looks friendly in one photograph. Spending time with it and discussing your circumstances can help you make a more responsible decision.
10: I want to experience a traditional summer festival in Japan because I enjoy learning how communities celebrate together. I hope to visit a town where local volunteers explain the activities to visitors. I hope that I can try a simple craft and learn the names of the materials involved. I wish I knew enough Japanese to understand longer conversations without needing every sentence translated. I wish I could read the signs easily when moving between different parts of the festival. My first step is to join a beginner language course and practice useful questions each week. I will also read information from the organizers before making travel plans. These preparations will not make me an expert, but they can help me participate more respectfully.
11: It has been raining steadily since early this morning, so our outdoor event cannot go ahead as planned. The rain has flooded part of the garden where we expected to place the tables. Several guests have already contacted us to ask whether the event is canceled. Before the weather changed, we had arranged the chairs and prepared signs for the entrance. We decided to move the gathering into the community hall instead of asking everyone to stay outside. My sister has been calling the remaining guests while I check that the hall is ready. The change is inconvenient, but the indoor space gives everyone a dry place to meet. We will keep the same starting time and explain the new entrance clearly in our messages.
12: When I arrived at our meeting room, I found the door locked and the lights switched off. The booking email confirms that our group reserved the room for this afternoon. The caretaker might be delayed because roadworks have disrupted traffic near the building. If she arrives soon, we will begin with the short presentation we prepared yesterday. If the room remains unavailable, we will meet in the cafe across the street instead. If I were the organizer, I would ask for an emergency contact number before the next meeting. I do not want to assume that someone forgot us without checking the facts first. For now, I will phone the office and explain that the group is waiting outside.
13: Our neighborhood has an unused garden that could become a pleasant shared space for residents. If we organize a cleanup on Saturday, we will be able to see which areas need repair. When the paths are clear, more people may feel comfortable walking through the garden after work. If several families volunteer regularly, we will have enough help to water the plants during dry weeks. We should begin with a small area rather than promise to improve everything at once. I hope we can arrange a monthly meeting where neighbors discuss practical needs and share suggestions. Some residents might prefer a quiet seating area, while others would enjoy growing vegetables. Listening to these different ideas can help us make a plan that people want to support.
14: My friends Ana and Luis have different personalities, but they share several important interests and values. Ana enjoys walking in the countryside, and so does Luis when he has a free weekend. Luis can explain difficult ideas patiently, and so can Ana when a classmate needs help. Ana does not like interrupting people during a conversation, and Luis does not either. Luis never enjoys making jokes at someone else's expense, and Ana does not either. They both value being kind because they remember how nervous they felt when joining our class. Ana usually speaks first when meeting new people, while Luis listens before joining in. Their friendship works well because they respect these differences instead of expecting each other to behave identically.
15: I try to keep a simple daily routine that leaves enough time for rest and ordinary activities. Before I leave home, I prepare some water and check what I need for the day. After I finish work, I usually take a comfortable walk with a friend in the nearby park. I enjoy this habit because it helps me separate the working day from my evening at home. Even though my schedule is sometimes busy, I avoid making the walk into a competition. If the path is slippery, I choose another route instead of rushing across it. In the evening, I prepare a meal and leave time to relax before bed. This is a description of my own routine, not a medical plan for someone with different needs.
16: When I was a teenager, I used to spend Saturday mornings helping my grandfather in his workshop. We used to repair old wooden toys that neighbors brought to his house. Every Saturday, he would show me one small task and wait patiently while I tried it myself. I enjoyed sanding the rough edges, although painting the tiny details required more patience than I had. At the end of the morning, we would clean the table and have lunch in the garden. Now I live in another city, and my weekends are usually filled with errands and study. I no longer work in that workshop regularly, but I still enjoy making simple things by hand. Those quiet mornings taught me to slow down and pay attention to small details.
17: Last year, I learned to repair a loose button on my coat by myself. I watched a short demonstration and practiced on an old shirt before touching the coat. My sister had taught herself the same skill, so she lent me some basic tools. She reminded me that I needed to be careful not to prick myself with the needle. If you want to teach yourself a practical skill, it helps to begin with a small task. Later, my brother and I challenged ourselves to mend other simple items instead of throwing them away. We did not become experts, but we became more confident about trying manageable repairs. I felt proud when the button stayed firmly attached during the following winter.
18: While I was carrying a tray through the kitchen, a cloth fell from the worktop in front of me. I stopped suddenly, and a small cup slid off the tray onto the floor. My sister was standing next to me, but fortunately the cup did not hit either of us. I checked myself for any cuts before moving away from the broken pieces. We kept everyone outside the kitchen while we carefully cleared the floor. The accident was small, but it reminded me to check the path before carrying several things at once. I also moved the loose cloth so that it could not fall into the walkway again. Afterward, we talked about arranging the kitchen so that everyday tasks would be less awkward.
19: During a study session, the person beside me kept playing videos loudly on a phone. I wanted to continue working without starting an argument in the shared room. I asked, "Could you tell me whether you have headphones with you?" The person said that the headphones were in a bag under the table. I then asked, "Would you mind using them while we finish this exercise?" Finally, I added, "Do you know where the quieter study area is if you need to make a call?" I chose polite questions because I wanted to explain the problem without embarrassing the other student. The person lowered the sound, found the headphones and apologized for disturbing the group.
20: This week, my friend and I discussed whether our class should organize an outdoor study meeting. She said that the park would give everyone more space to sit comfortably in small groups. I told her that some students might have difficulty hearing each other near the busy road. She answered, "We can choose a quieter corner beside the garden." I agreed that this was worth considering, but I still wanted a plan for rainy weather. We both liked the idea of changing our usual setting for one afternoon. However, we had different opinions about how much preparation the meeting would need. We decided to ask the group about accessibility and transport before choosing a location.
21: Yesterday, I talked to my colleague after the weekly team meeting at our office. We talked about the new schedule and how it would affect our lunch breaks. Later, our manager invited each person to speak briefly about a concern in a more formal discussion. I explained that a clearer timetable would help everyone plan their work without guessing when meetings would finish. My colleague agreed and suggested sharing the timetable at the beginning of each week. Speaking of schedules, we also need to decide when our English study group will meet next month. I will ask the other learners which evenings are convenient before booking a room. Our conversation showed me that informal talks and formal discussions can both lead to useful changes.
22: My aunt gave me useful advice when I was preparing for my first volunteer shift at the library. She told me to listen carefully before trying to answer a visitor's question too quickly. She also told me that asking a colleague for help was better than inventing an answer. She said that new volunteers are not expected to know every procedure immediately. Later, she said that a friendly attitude matters just as much as remembering where the books belong. She reminded me to tell the truth if I made a mistake while using the computer. I decided to say thank you by explaining how her advice helped me feel less nervous. During the shift, I remembered her words whenever I needed to pause and ask for guidance.
23: Next week, I will be helping our team prepare a small exhibition at the community center. On Monday morning, we will be arranging tables while the caretaker checks the lighting. At the same time on Tuesday, I will be labeling photographs and checking the order of the displays. On Wednesday afternoon, my colleague is going to be welcoming visitors at the main entrance. I will unlock the side door at two, which is one short action before the longer activities begin. During the evening, other volunteers will be explaining the displays to groups of visitors. We have divided the tasks so that nobody needs to do everything alone. I will check the final schedule on Sunday and tell the team if any arrangements need to change.
24: You had better read the course schedule carefully before paying for the weekend workshop. You had better not assume that all the materials are included in the advertised price. I would rather ask the organizer a few questions now than discover an unexpected cost later. The advanced session sounds interesting, but it may not match what we need to practice this month. I would rather join the beginner group because it gives us more time to understand each step. We can still watch a demonstration by the advanced group during the afternoon break. Choosing a suitable level is more useful than trying to impress people with a difficult project. Let us compare the two options calmly and make a decision after we receive the organizer's reply.
25: Before I changed jobs, I had been traveling across the city every morning for almost three years. I had been spending so much time on the bus that I rarely had energy for evening classes. My family had been encouraging me to look for work closer to home for several months. When a nearby company advertised a suitable position, I decided to prepare an application. I did not know whether I would succeed, but the opportunity matched the skills I already had. The interview went well, and I accepted an offer after discussing the schedule with the manager. Looking back, the long journey helped me understand how much I valued time for study and family. My new routine is less tiring, although learning a different job still takes patience and effort.
26: My cousins Paulo and Lucas look alike, especially when they wear similar jackets at family gatherings. They both look like their father, with dark hair and a very similar smile. Paulo is taller than Lucas, although the difference is difficult to notice in photographs. Lucas is a little more talkative than Paulo when they meet people for the first time. Paulo usually listens carefully before answering, while Lucas enjoys telling stories about his latest projects. Their voices are different too, so relatives rarely confuse them during a phone conversation. They sometimes joke about their similar appearance, but neither wants people to assume that their personalities are the same. Getting to know them separately makes the differences much easier to recognize.
27: I want to invite my friend to spend a relaxed afternoon at the park this weekend. Why don't we meet at the entrance after lunch and walk beside the lake? How about bringing a notebook so that we can practice describing the birds in English? I imagine that my friend might reply, "Thanks, but I have to help my family on Saturday afternoon." I could then suggest a different time instead of insisting on the original plan. Why don't we try Sunday morning, when the paths are usually quieter? If that is still inconvenient, we can arrange a short conversation online during the week. The invitation should give my friend an easy way to accept or decline without feeling pressured.
28: At our language school, students have to arrive before the teacher begins the listening activity. We ought to bring headphones when the class includes individual practice on the computers. We are supposed to leave the shared tables clean so that the next group can use them comfortably. Yesterday, I was supposed to return a borrowed workbook to the office before lunch. I forgot to bring it from home, so that expectation was not met. I explained the mistake to the administrator and arranged to return it the following morning. A clear rule tells us what is required, while advice can help us act more thoughtfully within those rules. I will check my bag tonight so that I can keep the new arrangement without another delay.
29: Our workplace has a written emergency procedure, and I want to understand it before a problem occurs. If the fire alarm sounds, I will follow the marked exit route and the building's instructions. If I notice that the usual route is blocked, I will follow the alternative route shown in the safety plan. I would not stop to collect my bag or try to investigate the source of the alarm. If I were you, I would ask the safety coordinator to explain the meeting point during the next orientation. Knowing the procedure in advance can reduce confusion when people need to act quickly. I would also report an unclear sign so that it could be corrected before an emergency. These examples describe following an existing workplace plan rather than replacing professional safety instructions.
30: I dream of traveling slowly through several countries and learning how people describe everyday life in different languages. I hope to become confident enough in English to ask thoughtful questions and understand the answers. At the moment, I plan to complete the next unit of my course and practice speaking twice a week. I have already chosen the study days and asked a friend to join one of the sessions. The travel idea remains a dream because I have not decided on a budget or a departure date. My study plan is more concrete because it includes specific actions that I can begin this week. I would love to turn the larger dream into a realistic trip in the future. For now, small regular steps give me a practical way to make progress without pretending that every detail is settled.
